docs.title: utils.crawl_local_files
docs.text:
utils/crawl_local_files.py

As the local filesystem counterpart to utils.crawl_github_files, this module provides directory traversal, file filtering, and content extraction capabilities for repositories stored locally on disk. It produces an output dictionary structure matching the remote GitHub crawler ({"files": {filepath: content}}), ensuring seamless interoperability across the ingestion pipeline.

docs.title: Technical Overview
docs.text: The module traverses local directories using a single-pass os.walk strategy with in-place directory pruning. During traversal, it respects git-ignore rules, glob inclusion/exclusion patterns, and file size limits, while safely extracting UTF-8 text content and discarding binary files.

docs.title: Key Capabilities
docs.text:
1. .gitignore Integration: Automatically detects and compiles repository-level .gitignore files using pathspec (with gitwildmatch syntax) to prune ignored paths before traversal.
  2. Directory Pruning: Mutates dirs in-place during os.walk execution to prevent traversing into excluded directory trees (e.g., .git, virtual environments, or node_modules).
  3. Filtering Pipeline: Applies exclusion patterns, inclusion filters, and size constraints sequentially to minimize unnecessary I/O operations.
  4. Encoding & Binary Safety: Reads file contents using utf-8-sig to automatically strip byte-order marks (BOM) while capturing UnicodeDecodeError and general exceptions to skip binary assets.
  5. ANSI Console Reporting: Emits formatted, color-coded logging for each encountered item and outputs a structured summary table at the end of the crawl process.

docs.title: crawl_local_files()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def crawl_local_files(directory, include_patterns=None, exclude_patterns=None, max_file_size=None, use_relative_paths=True)

Description: Crawls a local directory path, applying gitignore specifications, user-defined exclusion patterns, inclusion patterns, and file size restrictions. Files that pass all filter stages are read from disk using the utf-8-sig encoding format and stored in an internal dictionary indexed by their path.

Parameters: * directory (str): Target root filesystem path to crawl. * include_patterns (set | None): Optional set of glob patterns indicating which files should be included (e.g., {"*.py", "*.js"}). If provided, any file not matching at least one pattern is excluded. * exclude_patterns (set | None): Optional set of glob patterns indicating files or directories to skip (e.g., {"tests/*", "*.pyc"}). * max_file_size (int | None): Maximum allowed file size in bytes. Larger files are bypassed. * use_relative_paths (bool): If True, keys in the returned dictionary are relative to directory. If False, absolute/resolved filesystem paths are retained. Default is True.

Returns: * dict: A dictionary containing a single key "files", mapping string file paths to their read string contents: 

{"files": {filepath: content}}

Raises: * ValueError: Raised immediately if directory does not exist or is not recognized as a directory by os.path.isdir.

Implementation Logic:

    if not os.path.isdir(directory):
        raise ValueError(f"Directory does not exist: {directory}")

    files_dict = {}

    # --- ANSI colors ---
    C_GREEN = "\033[92m"
    C_GRAY = "\033[90m"
    C_RED = "\033[91m"
    C_RESET = "\033[0m"

    # --- Counters ---
    entry_num = 0
    count_processed = 0
    count_excluded = 0
    count_size_limit = 0
    count_non_text = 0
    skipped_size_limit = []
    skipped_non_text = []

    # --- Load .gitignore ---
    gitignore_path = os.path.join(directory, ".gitignore")
    gitignore_spec = None
    if os.path.exists(gitignore_path):
        try:
            with open(gitignore_path, encoding="utf-8-sig") as f:
                gitignore_patterns = f.readlines()
            gitignore_spec = pathspec.PathSpec.from_lines("gitwildmatch", gitignore_patterns)
            print(f"Loaded .gitignore patterns from {gitignore_path}")
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"Warning: Could not read or parse .gitignore file {gitignore_path}: {e}")
    # ...

The function initiates by validating the directory and preparing console logging tracking variables. It looks for a top-level .gitignore file within the specified directory. When found, it parses the ignore lines into a pathspec.PathSpec object using the gitwildmatch standard. Parsing errors are caught gracefully with a warning output, allowing the crawl to proceed even if .gitignore syntax is invalid or unreadable.

    # ...
    # --- Single-pass: walk, filter, and process inline ---
    for root, dirs, files in os.walk(directory):
        # --- Directory filtering ---
        excluded_dirs = set()
        for d in sorted(dirs):
            dirpath_rel = os.path.relpath(os.path.join(root, d), directory)

            reason = None
            if gitignore_spec and gitignore_spec.match_file(dirpath_rel):
                reason = "excluded (.gitignore)"
            elif exclude_patterns:
                for pattern in exclude_patterns:
                    dir_pattern = pattern.removesuffix("/*")
                    if fnmatch.fnmatch(dirpath_rel, dir_pattern) or fnmatch.fnmatch(d, dir_pattern):
                        reason = "excluded"
                        break

            if reason:
                excluded_dirs.add(d)
                entry_num += 1
                count_excluded += 1
                print(f"{C_GRAY}  [{entry_num}] {dirpath_rel}/ [{reason}]{C_RESET}")

        for d in dirs.copy():
            if d in excluded_dirs:
                dirs.remove(d)

        # Sort remaining dirs for consistent traversal order
        dirs.sort()
        # ...

For directory pruning, os.walk is traversed top-down. Candidate directory names in dirs are evaluated against both the parsed .gitignore pattern specification and the caller-provided exclude_patterns (handling patterns with or without trailing /*). Any directory matching an exclusion rule is collected in excluded_dirs and purged in-place from dirs via dirs.remove(d). This prevents os.walk from descending into unnecessary subtrees, significantly reducing crawl time on large repositories. Remaining directories are sorted in-place to guarantee deterministic traversal order.

        # ...
        # --- File processing (inline, sorted) ---
        for filename in sorted(files):
            filepath = os.path.join(root, filename)
            relpath = os.path.relpath(filepath, directory) if use_relative_paths else filepath
            entry_num += 1

            # Check gitignore
            if gitignore_spec and gitignore_spec.match_file(relpath):
                count_excluded += 1
                print(f"{C_GRAY}  [{entry_num}] {relpath} [excluded (.gitignore)]{C_RESET}")
                continue

            # Check exclude patterns
            excluded = False
            if exclude_patterns:
                for pattern in exclude_patterns:
                    if fnmatch.fnmatch(relpath, pattern):
                        excluded = True
                        break
            if excluded:
                count_excluded += 1
                print(f"{C_GRAY}  [{entry_num}] {relpath} [excluded]{C_RESET}")
                continue

            # Check include patterns
            if include_patterns:
                matched = False
                for pattern in include_patterns:
                    if fnmatch.fnmatch(relpath, pattern):
                        matched = True
                        break
                if not matched:
                    count_excluded += 1
                    print(f"{C_GRAY}  [{entry_num}] {relpath} [excluded (not in include list)]{C_RESET}")
                    continue

            # Check size limit
            if max_file_size and os.path.getsize(filepath) > max_file_size:
                count_size_limit += 1
                skipped_size_limit.append(relpath)
                size_kb = os.path.getsize(filepath) / 1024
                print(f"{C_RED}  [{entry_num}] {relpath} [size limit: {size_kb:.0f}KB]{C_RESET}")
                continue

            # Try to read as text
            try:
                with open(filepath, encoding="utf-8-sig") as f:
                    content = f.read()
                files_dict[relpath] = content
                count_processed += 1
                print(f"{C_GREEN}  [{entry_num}] {relpath} [processed]{C_RESET}")
            except (UnicodeDecodeError, ValueError):
                count_non_text += 1
                skipped_non_text.append(relpath)
                print(f"{C_RED}  [{entry_num}] {relpath} [cannot process: not a text file]{C_RESET}")
            except Exception as e:
                count_non_text += 1
                skipped_non_text.append(relpath)
                print(f"{C_RED}  [{entry_num}] {relpath} [cannot process: {e}]{C_RESET}")
    # ...

Files within each directory are evaluated in sorted order. For each candidate file: 1. It is matched against .gitignore using pathspec.match_file(). 2. It is checked against caller-provided exclude_patterns using fnmatch.fnmatch(). 3. If include_patterns is provided, the path must match at least one inclusion pattern; otherwise, it is skipped. 4. If max_file_size is specified and the file's disk size exceeds this threshold, the file is skipped and logged with its size in kilobytes. 5. If all checks pass, the file is opened with utf-8-sig encoding. If the file is binary or has an incompatible encoding, a UnicodeDecodeError or ValueError is caught, and the path is cataloged in skipped_non_text. Any other filesystem I/O exceptions are caught and reported as non-text errors without crashing the crawler.

    # ...
    # --- Summary ---
    total_fetched = count_processed + count_excluded + count_size_limit + count_non_text
    print("\n--- Crawl Summary ---")
    print(f"  Total found : {total_fetched}")
    print(f"{C_GREEN}  Processed   : {count_processed}{C_RESET}")
    if count_excluded > 0:
        print(f"{C_GRAY}  Excluded    : {count_excluded}{C_RESET}")
    if count_size_limit > 0:
        print(f"{C_RED}  Size limit  : {count_size_limit}{C_RESET}")
        for f in skipped_size_limit:
            print(f"{C_RED}    - {f}{C_RESET}")
    if count_non_text > 0:
        print(f"{C_RED}  Non-text    : {count_non_text}{C_RESET}")
        for f in skipped_non_text:
            print(f"{C_RED}    - {f}{C_RESET}")
    print("---------------------")

    return {"files": files_dict}

Once os.walk finishes traversing the target directory tree, crawl_local_files aggregates statistics for total entries found, successfully processed files, excluded items, files exceeding the size threshold, and non-text/unreadable files. It prints this detailed breakdown to standard output and returns the final dictionary.

Usage Example:

# Extract from utils/crawl_local_files.py (__main__ execution block)
if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("--- Crawling parent directory ('..') ---")
    files_data = crawl_local_files(
        "..",
        exclude_patterns={
            "*.pyc",
            "__pycache__/*",
            ".venv/*",
            ".git/*",
            "docs/*",
            "output/*",
        },
    )
    print(f"Found {len(files_data['files'])} files:")
    for path in files_data["files"]:
        print(f"  {path}")

docs.title: Technical Overview
docs.text:
The crawl_local_files.py module serves as the local filesystem ingestion engine for the Codebase-Knowledge-Builder pipeline. While remote codebase ingestion is delegated to crawl_github_files.py, crawl_local_files.py provides an in-memory extraction pipeline tailored for local directories. It navigates directory trees, applies hierarchical ignore rules, prunes unwanted directory branches early, enforces file size thresholds, decodes text files across heterogeneous character encodings, and streams real-time telemetry back to the user interface.

Operating directly on the host operating system's virtual file system (VFS), the crawler standardizes file representations across platforms by normalizing path separators and handling character encoding quirks (such as UTF-8 Byte Order Marks). It abstracts away low-level filesystem traversal complexities, returning an ingestion payload structure compatible with downstream analysis modules.

docs.title: Key Capabilities and Operational Characteristics
docs.text:
1. Cascading Hierarchical .gitignore Resolution: The crawler dynamically loads root-level and nested .gitignore files encountered at any directory depth during traversal. It creates isolated pathspec.PathSpec evaluation scopes bound to their originating directory trees, preserving Git's contextual inheritance and override semantics.
  2. Early Subtree Pruning: During directory traversal via os.walk, the module modifies directory collections in-place. If a directory matches ignore rules or exclusion globs, it is pruned immediately, preventing unnecessary recursive traversal into large subtrees such as node_modules, .git, or build artifact directories.
  3. Multi-Stage File Filtering Pipeline: Individual files are evaluated against a strict sequence of filters: scoped .gitignore rule matching, user-defined exclude_patterns, user-defined include_patterns, and filesystem byte size limits (max_file_size).
  4. Resilient Text Ingestion and Encoding Fallback: Files are read using utf-8-sig decoding to automatically strip UTF-8 BOM headers. If decoding fails due to UnicodeDecodeError or ValueError (indicating binary or corrupted assets), the crawler logs the file as skipped without terminating the crawl.
  5. Real-Time Structured Telemetry: Telemetry and progress indicators are emitted through utils.output (emit and get), tracking processed counts, exclusions, file size ceiling violations, and binary skips.

docs.title: _load_gitignore()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private (_) Signature: def _load_gitignore(gitignore_path: str) -> pathspec.PathSpec | None

Description: Attempts to open, read, and compile a .gitignore file located at gitignore_path into an immutable pathspec.PathSpec object using the standard Git wildmatch pattern syntax (gitwildmatch).

Under the hood, the function opens the target file using the utf-8-sig encoding, which automatically detects and removes any leading UTF-8 Byte Order Marks (BOMs) that might otherwise corrupt pattern parsing on Windows systems. If the file cannot be accessed due to filesystem permissions, OS-level locks, missing files, or corrupt encodings, the function swallows the exception and returns None, ensuring that an unreadable ignore file does not halt the crawling pipeline.

Parameters: * gitignore_path (str): Absolute or relative filesystem path to the .gitignore file.

Returns: * pathspec.PathSpec | None: A compiled PathSpec pattern matcher instance if successfully loaded and parsed; otherwise None.

Raises: * None: All internal exceptions (e.g., IOError, OSError, UnicodeDecodeError) are caught and handled by returning None.

Example: 

def _load_gitignore(gitignore_path):
    """Load a .gitignore file and return a PathSpec, or None on failure."""
    try:
        with open(gitignore_path, encoding="utf-8-sig") as f:
            return pathspec.PathSpec.from_lines("gitwildmatch", f.readlines())
    except Exception:
        return None

The function reads the entire contents of the .gitignore file into a list of strings using f.readlines(). It delegates parsing to pathspec.PathSpec.from_lines("gitwildmatch", ...), which parses comment lines (#), negation markers (!), directory path indicators (/), and glob wildcards (*, **, ?). The resulting PathSpec instance encapsulates the parsed pattern logic, ready for path matching operations.

docs.title: _matches_any_gitignore()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private (_) Signature: def _matches_any_gitignore(gitignore_specs: dict[str, pathspec.PathSpec], abs_path: str, is_dir: bool = False) -> bool

Description: Determines whether a given absolute path matches any active .gitignore specification within an arbitrary directory hierarchy. The function maintains Git's directory-scoped matching rules, ensuring that a .gitignore spec only applies to files and directories located within its own subtree.

The function iterates over the gitignore_specs dictionary (mapping abs_dir_path to its compiled pathspec.PathSpec). For each spec, it computes the relative path of abs_path against abs_dir_path using os.path.relpath. If the relative path starts with .., the target file or directory is outside the scope of that .gitignore and is skipped.

For targets within scope, Windows backslashes (\) are converted to standard POSIX forward slashes (/). If is_dir is True, a trailing slash (/) is enforced, which allows gitwildmatch to evaluate directory-specific rules (such as build/ matching directories but not files named build). The function returns True upon the first matching spec.

Parameters: * gitignore_specs (dict[str, pathspec.PathSpec]): Mapping of absolute directory paths to their respective compiled PathSpec pattern instances. * abs_path (str): The absolute path of the candidate file or directory to check. * is_dir (bool, optional): Flag indicating whether abs_path refers to a directory (True) or a file (False). Defaults to False.

Returns: * bool: True if abs_path matches any active .gitignore rule within its hierarchy; otherwise False.

Raises: * None: Operates deterministically over in-memory strings and path specs without raising exceptions.

Example: 

def _matches_any_gitignore(gitignore_specs, abs_path, is_dir=False):
    """Check if a path matches ANY loaded .gitignore spec.

    Each spec is checked with the path relative to its own .gitignore directory.
    For directories, a trailing '/' is appended for proper gitignore matching.

    Args:
        gitignore_specs: dict of {abs_dir_path: pathspec.PathSpec}
        abs_path: absolute path of the file or directory to check
        is_dir: True if checking a directory
    Returns:
        True if the path matches any gitignore rule
    """
    for gi_dir, spec in gitignore_specs.items():
        rel = os.path.relpath(abs_path, gi_dir)
        # Skip if the path is not under this gitignore's scope
        if rel.startswith(".."):
            continue
        match_path = rel.replace("\\", "/")
        if is_dir:
            match_path = match_path.rstrip("/") + "/"
        if spec.match_file(match_path):
            return True
    return False

This method implements Git's hierarchical scoping mechanics. By evaluating rel.startswith(".."), it prevents higher-level specs from evaluating upward and ensures that sibling or parent directories do not misapply child .gitignore rules. The directory trailing slash normalization (match_path.rstrip("/") + "/") ensures compatibility with the gitwildmatch standard, where patterns like dist/ specifically require a trailing slash to identify directories.

docs.title: crawl_local_files()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def crawl_local_files(directory: str, include_patterns: set[str] | None = None, exclude_patterns: set[str] | None = None, max_file_size: int | None = None, use_relative_paths: bool = True) -> dict[str, dict[str, str]]

Description: Executes a filtered traversal of a local filesystem directory, returning an in-memory dictionary of relative file paths mapped to their text contents. It provides a standardized data contract equivalent to remote crawlers such as crawl_github_files.py.

The crawling lifecycle proceeds through distinct phases: 1. Validation & Initialization: Validates that directory exists and is a directory. Pre-loads the root .gitignore if present and initializes telemetry counters. 2. Directory-Level Pruning: Dynamically loads any nested .gitignore files encountered during os.walk. Evaluates directories against ignore specs and exclude_patterns, modifying the dirs list in-place to prune subtrees immediately. 3. File-Level Filtering: Evaluates each file against .gitignore specs, exclude_patterns, include_patterns, and max_file_size. 4. Content Extraction: Opens qualifying files with utf-8-sig decoding. Skips binary or unreadable files upon encountering UnicodeDecodeError or ValueError. 5. Telemetry Reporting: Emits crawl metrics (processed, excluded, size limit exceeded, non-text) via utils.output.emit.

Parameters: * directory (str): Target local filesystem path to crawl. * include_patterns (set[str] | None, optional): Set of glob patterns (e.g., {"*.py", "*.ts"}) that files must match to be included. If None or empty, all non-excluded files are accepted. * exclude_patterns (set[str] | None, optional): Set of glob patterns (e.g., {"tests/*", "*.lock"}) to exclude from traversal. * max_file_size (int | None, optional): Maximum allowed file size in bytes. Files exceeding this ceiling are skipped. If None, no size ceiling is enforced. * use_relative_paths (bool, optional): Whether to use paths relative to directory as keys in the returned dictionary (True), or absolute system paths (False). Defaults to True.

Returns: * dict[str, dict[str, str]]: A dictionary payload containing a "files" dictionary mapping file paths to their decoded string contents: 

{
    "files": {
        "src/main.py": "import os\n...",
        "README.md": "# Documentation\n..."
    }
}

Raises: * ValueError: Raised if directory does not exist or is not a valid directory.

docs.title: Implementation Walkthrough: Initialization and Root Setup
docs.text:
if not os.path.isdir(directory):
        raise ValueError(f"Directory does not exist: {directory}")

    files_dict = {}

    # --- Counters ---
    entry_num = 0
    count_processed = 0
    count_excluded = 0
    count_size_limit = 0
    count_non_text = 0
    skipped_size_limit = []
    skipped_non_text = []

    # --- Gitignore specs: {abs_dir_path: pathspec} ---
    gitignore_specs = {}
    root_gi_path = os.path.join(directory, ".gitignore")
    if os.path.exists(root_gi_path):
        spec = _load_gitignore(root_gi_path)
        if spec:
            gitignore_specs[os.path.abspath(directory)] = spec
            emit("CRAWL_GITIGNORE_LOADED", path=root_gi_path)

    # Translated reason strings (looked up once)
    reason_excluded = get("CRAWL_REASON_EXCLUDED")
    reason_gitignore = get("CRAWL_REASON_GITIGNORE")

The function begins with defensive validation via os.path.isdir(). It initializes tracking counters and lists for telemetry reporting. Before beginning directory traversal, it checks for a root .gitignore, loading it into gitignore_specs indexed by the absolute path of the root directory. Reason strings for telemetry are resolved up-front via get() to prevent repeated dictionary lookups during deep tree traversals.

docs.title: Implementation Walkthrough: Directory Branch Pruning
docs.text:
# --- Single-pass: walk, filter, and process inline ---
    for root, dirs, files in os.walk(directory):
        abs_root = os.path.abspath(root)

        # Check for nested .gitignore in current directory (skip root, already loaded)
        if abs_root != os.path.abspath(directory):
            nested_gi = os.path.join(root, ".gitignore")
            if os.path.exists(nested_gi):
                spec = _load_gitignore(nested_gi)
                if spec:
                    gitignore_specs[abs_root] = spec

        # --- Directory filtering ---
        excluded_dirs = set()
        for d in sorted(dirs):
            abs_d = os.path.join(abs_root, d)
            dirpath_rel = os.path.relpath(abs_d, directory)

            reason = None
            if _matches_any_gitignore(gitignore_specs, abs_d, is_dir=True):
                reason = reason_gitignore
            elif exclude_patterns:
                for pattern in exclude_patterns:
                    dir_pattern = pattern.removesuffix("/*")
                    if fnmatch.fnmatch(dirpath_rel, dir_pattern) or fnmatch.fnmatch(d, dir_pattern):
                        reason = reason_excluded
                        break

            if reason:
                excluded_dirs.add(d)
                entry_num += 1
                count_excluded += 1
                emit("CRAWL_DIR_EXCLUDED", num=entry_num, path=dirpath_rel, reason=reason)

        for d in dirs.copy():
            if d in excluded_dirs:
                dirs.remove(d)

        # Sort remaining dirs for consistent traversal order
        dirs.sort()

This block performs in-place directory pruning during os.walk. For each traversed directory, it discovers any nested .gitignore files and registers them within gitignore_specs. It then iterates through the child directory names (dirs), checking each against loaded .gitignore specs and user-defined exclude_patterns (normalizing wildcard suffixes like /*).

Directories marked for exclusion are pruned in-place by removing them from dirs via dirs.remove(d). This prevents os.walk from descending into those subtrees on subsequent iterations. The remaining directories are sorted to guarantee deterministic, reproducible traversal orders across different operating systems.

docs.title: Implementation Walkthrough: File Filtering and Text Extraction
docs.text:
# --- File processing (inline, sorted) ---
        for filename in sorted(files):
            filepath = os.path.join(root, filename)
            abs_filepath = os.path.abspath(filepath)
            relpath = os.path.relpath(filepath, directory) if use_relative_paths else filepath
            entry_num += 1

            # Check gitignore (all levels)
            if _matches_any_gitignore(gitignore_specs, abs_filepath):
                count_excluded += 1
                emit("CRAWL_FILE_GITIGNORE", num=entry_num, path=relpath)
                continue

            # Check exclude patterns
            excluded = False
            if exclude_patterns:
                for pattern in exclude_patterns:
                    if fnmatch.fnmatch(relpath, pattern):
                        excluded = True
                        break
            if excluded:
                count_excluded += 1
                emit("CRAWL_FILE_EXCLUDED", num=entry_num, path=relpath)
                continue

            # Check include patterns
            if include_patterns:
                matched = False
                for pattern in include_patterns:
                    if fnmatch.fnmatch(relpath, pattern):
                        matched = True
                        break
                if not matched:
                    count_excluded += 1
                    emit("CRAWL_FILE_NOT_INCLUDED", num=entry_num, path=relpath)
                    continue

            # Check size limit
            if max_file_size and os.path.getsize(filepath) > max_file_size:
                count_size_limit += 1
                skipped_size_limit.append(relpath)
                size_kb = os.path.getsize(filepath) / 1024
                emit("CRAWL_FILE_SIZE_LIMIT", num=entry_num, path=relpath, size=f"{size_kb:.0f}")
                continue

            # Try to read as text
            try:
                with open(filepath, encoding="utf-8-sig") as f:
                    content = f.read()
                files_dict[relpath] = content
                count_processed += 1
                emit("CRAWL_FILE_PROCESSED", num=entry_num, path=relpath)
            except (UnicodeDecodeError, ValueError):
                count_non_text += 1
                skipped_non_text.append(relpath)
                emit("CRAWL_FILE_NOT_TEXT", num=entry_num, path=relpath)
            except Exception as e:
                count_non_text += 1
                skipped_non_text.append(relpath)
                emit("CRAWL_FILE_ERROR", num=entry_num, path=relpath, error=e)

File evaluation proceeds through a sequence of guard conditions. Candidate files are checked against _matches_any_gitignore(), then against glob expressions in exclude_patterns, and then against include_patterns. Files exceeding max_file_size are skipped and tracked in skipped_size_limit.

Qualifying files are read into memory using open(filepath, encoding="utf-8-sig"). If reading fails due to a UnicodeDecodeError or ValueError, the file is identified as binary or unreadable and recorded in skipped_non_text. Any unexpected filesystem errors (e.g., race-condition permission changes) are caught, emitted as CRAWL_FILE_ERROR, and skipped without crashing the traversal loop.

docs.title: Implementation Walkthrough: Summary Telemetry and Return
docs.text:
# --- Summary ---
    total_fetched = count_processed + count_excluded + count_size_limit + count_non_text
    emit("CRAWL_SUMMARY_HEADER")
    emit("CRAWL_SUMMARY_TOTAL", count=total_fetched)
    emit("CRAWL_SUMMARY_PROCESSED", count=count_processed)
    if count_excluded > 0:
        emit("CRAWL_SUMMARY_EXCLUDED", count=count_excluded)
    if count_size_limit > 0:
        emit("CRAWL_SUMMARY_SIZE_LIMIT", count=count_size_limit)
        for f in skipped_size_limit:
            emit("CRAWL_SUMMARY_ITEM", name=f)
    if count_non_text > 0:
        emit("CRAWL_SUMMARY_NON_TEXT", count=count_non_text)
        for f in skipped_non_text:
            emit("CRAWL_SUMMARY_ITEM", name=f)

    return {"files": files_dict}

Once traversal completes, the function aggregates its counters and emits a structured summary through emit(). It reports the total number of evaluated entries, successfully processed files, exclusions, size ceiling violations, and binary skips, including individual file paths for skipped items. Finally, it returns the standard payload dictionary containing the accumulated files_dict.

docs.title: Standalone Execution Block
docs.text:
The module includes an execution block enabling standalone CLI invocation for testing and debugging directory traversals:

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("--- Crawling parent directory ('..') ---")
    files_data = crawl_local_files(
        "..",
        exclude_patterns={
            "*.pyc",
            "__pycache__/*",
            ".venv/*",
            ".git/*",
            "docs/*",
            "output/*",
        },
    )
    print(f"Found {len(files_data['files'])} files:")
    for path in files_data["files"]:
        print(f"  {path}")

When executed directly (python utils/crawl_local_files.py), the script targets the parent directory (..) while excluding standard virtual environments, cache directories, Git metadata, and output artifacts. It logs the total count and relative paths of all discovered, non-excluded text files to standard output.

docs.title: Pipeline Context and Data Flow
docs.text:
The following sequence diagram illustrates how crawl_local_files.py interacts with the host filesystem and the telemetry subsystem during a crawl triggered by downstream consumers (such as pipeline nodes in nodes.py):

sequenceDiagram

    participant Caller as Orchestrator (nodes.py / main.py)
    participant Crawler as crawl_local_files()
    participant FS as Host File System (VFS)
    participant Output as utils.output (emit)

    end

docs.title: Error Handling and Edge Cases
docs.text: Scenario / Condition Handling Mechanism Pipeline Impact Non-Existent Target Path os.path.isdir() check raises ValueError immediately. Traversal is aborted before any filesystem operations occur. Malformed / Unreadable .gitignore Handled in _load_gitignore() via try...except Exception, which catches the error and returns None. The unreadable ignore file is skipped; traversal continues without applying those specific rules. Windows Path Separators (\) Normalized in _matches_any_gitignore() via .replace("\\", "/"). Ensures consistent glob matching against POSIX-based .gitignore specifications across platforms. Directory Ignores with Trailing Slash _matches_any_gitignore() appends / when is_dir=True. Complies with gitwildmatch specifications (e.g., build/ matches directories but not files named build). Out-of-Scope Nested Ignore Rules Handled via rel.startswith("..") check in _matches_any_gitignore(). Prevents nested .gitignore files from matching paths outside their parent directory tree. Binary and Compiled Files Handled in open() block by catching (UnicodeDecodeError, ValueError). The file is skipped, recorded in skipped_non_text, and traversal continues. Files Exceeding max_file_size Checked via os.path.getsize(filepath) > max_file_size before opening. Content is not read into memory, preventing memory spikes and token window overflow. Filesystem Race Conditions Handled via generic except Exception as e block wrapping file reads. Emits CRAWL_FILE_ERROR with the exception details and continues traversal.

docs.title: Performance Characteristics and Resource Management
docs.text:
1. Memory Complexity: The memory footprint scales with the aggregate size of all ingested text file contents stored in files_dict. Files excluded by pattern or size limits are never read into memory, keeping heap allocation proportional only to valid source files.
  2. I/O Complexity and Subtree Pruning: Modifying the dirs list in-place during os.walk avoids traversing into excluded directory trees entirely (such as .git or node_modules). This eliminates unnecessary stat and read system calls on large subtrees.
  3. Regex and Pattern Caching: pathspec.PathSpec compiles wildmatch expressions into regular expressions upon initialization. Because .gitignore files are parsed once per directory and retained in gitignore_specs, pattern matching operations run efficiently against pre-compiled expressions.

docs.title: exclude_patterns.py
docs.text:
Source: utils/exclude_patterns.py

Following the filesystem traversal mechanics established in crawl_local_files.py, the exclude_patterns.py module defines the baseline exclusion rules used across both local and remote repository crawling pipelines. It acts as the central filtering configuration for preventing context window exhaustion, unparseable binary ingestion, credential leaks, and redundant build artifact parsing within the Codebase-Knowledge-Builder system.

docs.title: Technical Overview
docs.text:
The primary responsibility of utils/exclude_patterns.py is to declare DEFAULT_EXCLUDE_PATTERNS, an immutable baseline configuration set of glob rules formatted according to standard Unix shell wildcard syntax (fnmatch). When building knowledge graphs and architecture representations via Large Language Models (LLMs), feeding irrelevant, auto-generated, or excessively large binary files degrades generation quality and rapidly depletes input token quotas.

This module centralizes filtering declarations into a unified constant. Rather than relying solely on repository-specific .gitignore files—which are frequently absent, misconfigured, or inadequate for LLM context curation—the rules defined here establish an aggressive, domain-aware pruning baseline.

docs.title: Key Architectural Responsibilities
docs.text:
1. Token Window Protection: Automatically skips dependency directories (e.g., node_modules/, venv/), package lockfiles (e.g., package-lock.json, poetry.lock), and framework build caches (e.g., .next/, target/, dist/) that contain millions of redundant or auto-generated tokens.
  2. Binary and Media Rejection: Filters out non-text static assets (e.g., .png, .mp4, .pdf, .zip, .tar.gz) and compiled object code (.pyc, .class, .dll, .so, .exe), preventing decoding failures and memory overhead during file reads.
  3. Secret and Environment Sanitization: Blocks root and nested environmental variable files (.env, .env.*) from entering prompt generation pipelines, avoiding accidental leakage of API credentials and cryptographic secrets.
  4. Tooling and Agent Workspace Isolation: Excludes metadata, cache stores, and instruction sets from modern AI IDEs and agents (e.g., .cursor/, .windsurf/, .cline/, .agent/, .continue/), ensuring the LLM analyzes the actual software architecture rather than ephemeral agent state files.

docs.title: Pattern Evaluation Pipeline
docs.text:
The rules in DEFAULT_EXCLUDE_PATTERNS are evaluated during directory discovery and file matching in both crawl_local_files.py and crawl_github_files.py. The matching logic operates in two distinct tiers: directory-level subtree pruning and file-level path filtering.

flowchart TD
    subgraph S1["1. Local Traversal (os.walk)"]
        A["Inspect Discovered Directory"] --> B{"Directory matches pattern/*?"}
        B -- Yes --> C["Mutate dirs list in-place (Prune descent)"]
        B -- No --> D["Inspect Discovered File"]
        D --> E{"Filename matches pattern or *.ext?"}
        E -- Yes --> F["Skip File Reading"]
        E -- No --> G["Proceed to .gitignore and Size Validation"]
    end

    subgraph S2["2. Remote Traversal (GitHub API/Git)"]
        H["Inspect Git Tree Entry"] --> I{"Path matches directory pattern/*?"}
        I -- Yes --> J["Omit recursive tree fetch"]
        I -- No --> K{"Path matches file pattern?"}
        K -- Yes --> L["Omit blob payload download"]
        K -- No --> M["Queue blob download and UTF-8 decoding"]
    end

docs.title: DEFAULT_EXCLUDE_PATTERNS
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Type: set[str] Signature: 

DEFAULT_EXCLUDE_PATTERNS: set[str]

Description: A constant Python set of strings containing glob patterns compatible with fnmatch.fnmatch() and standard Unix globbing. The collection encompasses 7 distinct categories of files and directories that are omitted by default during repository ingestion.

Directory patterns explicitly terminate with a trailing /* wildcard. Crawlers inspect directory names against stripped variants of these patterns (or evaluate the directory path suffixed with /*) to immediately prune entire directory subtrees from the traversal stack prior to disk or network I/O. File patterns utilize leading wildcard extensions (*.ext), exact base names (e.g., .DS_Store), or prefix wildcards (e.g., .env.*).

docs.title: Detailed Category Breakdown
docs.text: The DEFAULT_EXCLUDE_PATTERNS set is logically partitioned into 7 functional domains in the source code. The following subsections detail each category, showing the exact source code slices and explaining the underlying architectural rationale.

docs.title: Behavior & Rationale
docs.text:
This category excludes raster and vector graphics, audio/video streams, office documents, compressed archive formats, and standard static asset storage directories.

  • Binary Safety: Non-text assets (such as .png, .zip, .pdf) cannot be meaningfully interpreted by source code analysis prompts without specialized multimodal parsing. Ingesting these files triggers UnicodeDecodeError exceptions in text-oriented ingestion pipelines.
  • Payload Volume: Compressed archives (.zip, .tar.gz) and multimedia files (.mp4, .mov) contain multi-megabyte payloads that would quickly exceed crawler memory buffers and API transmission boundaries.
  • Subtree Pruning: Common static directory paths such as public/*, static/*, and assets/* are bypassed entirely, eliminating hundreds of client-side web assets (favicons, bundled stylesheets, icons) that carry minimal structural information about core business logic.

docs.title: Behavior & Rationale
docs.text:
This category targets compilation artifacts, transpile targets, framework server-side rendering (SSR) caches, documentation output directories, and temporary editor swap files.

  • Frontend & Modern Frameworks: Directories like .next/*, .nuxt/*, and .svelte-kit/* store generated JavaScript chunks, prerendered HTML manifests, and client-side hydration maps created during local development runs.
  • Compiled Target Directories: Standard build output locations like target/* (Rust/Cargo/Maven), bin/* and obj/* (.NET/C#), and dist/* / build/* (C/C++, Python wheels, npm packages) contain duplicated or compiled copies of source files already present in primary source directories.
  • Documentation and Non-Core Code: Directories such as docs/*, examples/*, test/*, tests/*, deprecated/*, and legacy/* are excluded to maintain a high signal-to-noise ratio in the generated architecture knowledge base, focusing the LLM's attention on active production code.
  • Ephemeral Files: Matchers like *.log, *.tmp, *.bak, and *.swp (Vim swap files) prevent ingestion of volatile runtime data.

docs.title: Behavior & Rationale
docs.text:
This partition prevents third-party package dependencies, virtual environment trees, environment secret files, and dependency lockfiles from contaminating the knowledge pipeline.

  • Dependency Directory Pruning: The presence of node_modules/*, vendor/* (PHP/Composer or Go), or venv/* / .venv/* (Python) can introduce tens of thousands of third-party source files into the crawl. Pruning these subtrees reduces traversal duration from minutes to milliseconds.
  • Lockfile Exclusions: Detailed dependency tree resolutions (e.g., package-lock.json, yarn.lock, Cargo.lock, poetry.lock) frequently span tens of thousands of lines of machine-generated metadata. Analyzing them provides low architectural value while consuming massive token budgets.
  • Secret Protection: Patterns matching .env and .env.* (e.g., .env.local, .env.production) ensure runtime credentials, database connection strings, and API keys are never captured in crawler payloads or transmitted to external LLM providers.

docs.title: Behavior & Rationale
docs.text:
This category isolates language-specific bytecode, testing caches, compilation intermediate outputs, shared dynamic libraries, and mobile native build environments.

  • Python Runtime & Tooling: Excludes bytecode files (*.pyc, *.pyo), C extensions (*.pyd), compilation directories (__pycache__/*), and analysis tool caches (.pytest_cache/*, .ruff_cache/*, .tox/*, .coverage, htmlcov/*).
  • Java Virtual Machine (JVM): Excludes compiled Java bytecode (*.class), Java archives (*.jar, *.war, *.ear, *.nar), and Gradle dependency caches (.gradle/*).
  • Native C/C++/Rust Artifacts: Strips compiled machine code object files (*.o, *.obj), static libraries (*.a, *.lib), shared libraries (*.so, *.dylib, *.dll), and compiled executables (*.exe).
  • Mobile Subsystems: Bypasses CocoaPods dependency trees (ios/Pods/*) and Android Gradle compilation directories (android/.gradle/*, android/app/build/*).

docs.title: Behavior & Rationale
docs.text:
This category handles operating system metadata files and version control management internals.

  • VCS Internals: Suppresses the internal database directories of version control systems, including Git (.git/*), Subversion (.svn/*), and Mercurial (.hg/*). It also excludes GitHub-specific configuration trees (.github/*, which includes CI/CD workflow YAMLs, issue templates, and dependabot configurations) to focus ingestion strictly on functional source code.
  • Operating System Metadata: Filters out macOS Finder metadata (.DS_Store), Windows Explorer thumbnail caches (Thumbs.db), and Windows folder customization files (desktop.ini), preventing platform-specific system artifacts from polluting cross-platform code crawls.

This category covers project and workspace configurations generated by traditional integrated development environments.

  • JetBrains & IntelliJ Platform: Matches .idea/* settings trees and project module files (*.iml).
  • Visual Studio & VS Code: Ignores .vscode/* workspace configurations (such as launch.json, settings.json, and tasks.json) as well as Visual Studio solution caches (.vs/*).
  • Eclipse Foundation: Excludes Eclipse project files (.project, .classpath) and internal preferences directories (.eclipse/*, .settings/*).

docs.title: Behavior & Rationale
docs.text:
This section provides rules targeting AI development tools, coding assistants, and autonomous agent frameworks.

  • Rule Definitions: Files such as .cursorrules, .windsurfrules, .clinerules, and .roorules contain custom system instructions and behavior guidelines for IDE assistant plugins. Excluding them ensures that the downstream LLM analyzes codebase logic without being influenced or confused by instructions written for other AI tools.
  • Agent Scratchpads and State Trees: Directories like .cursor/*, .windsurf/*, .cline/*, .roo/*, .agent/*, .agents/*, .continue/*, .aide/*, .gemini/*, .antigravity/*, .claude/*, and .copilot/* store local conversation histories, indexed vector stores, shadow workspaces, and execution state trees. Excluding these prevents cyclical prompting loops and large metadata ingestions.

docs.title: Comparative Pattern Classification
docs.text:
The patterns declared in DEFAULT_EXCLUDE_PATTERNS follow four specific glob matching formats, each evaluated through distinct logic in the ingestion engines:

Pattern Syntax Type Examples Matching Mechanism Crawler Application Directory Wildcard (dir/*) node_modules/*, dist/*, .git/* Matches directory paths directly. The suffix /* is stripped during directory-level evaluation. Used in os.walk() to prune dirs in-place, skipping entire subtrees before child traversal. File Extension Wildcard (*.ext) *.jpg, *.pyc, *.lock, *.class fnmatch.fnmatch(filename, "*.ext") or checking file suffixes. Evaluated against individual file names during directory iterations. Exact File Match (name) .DS_Store, .cursorrules, .env Exact string equality filename == pattern or fnmatch.fnmatch(filename, pattern). Checked against base filenames to eliminate system and configuration files. Prefix / Infix Wildcard (prefix*) .env.*, output-test*/* Evaluated against relative paths or filenames using fnmatch. Blocks variable-named files like .env.development or dynamic test output directories.

docs.title: Consumption in crawl_local_files.py
docs.text: In crawl_local_files.py, DEFAULT_EXCLUDE_PATTERNS is loaded as the base exclusion set. During traversal with os.walk(), directory entries are evaluated against these patterns (stripping the trailing /* for directory comparisons). Matching subdirectories are removed directly from the dirs list, which prevents os.walk() from descending into those directories. Individual files are subsequently checked against file-level glob patterns using fnmatch.fnmatch().

docs.title: Consumption in crawl_github_files.py
docs.text: In crawl_github_files.py, DEFAULT_EXCLUDE_PATTERNS is combined with repository .gitignore definitions using pathspec or fnmatch filters. When inspecting tree structures retrieved from the GitHub REST API or local temporary Git clones, paths matching these exclusion rules are discarded before blob retrieval, reducing API usage and transfer overhead.

docs.title: output.py
docs.text:
Source: utils/output.py

Following the baseline filesystem filtering rules established in exclude_patterns.py to discard extraneous files during codebase crawling, the Codebase-Knowledge-Builder pipeline requires a unified telemetry, logging, and user communication interface. The output.py module serves as this centralized subsystem, managing ANSI-styled terminal output, persistent file logging, multi-language internationalization (i18n), dynamic LLM-driven string translation, and UI string retrieval for generated documentation artifacts.

docs.title: Technical Overview
docs.text:
The output.py module centralizes all visual presentation, diagnostic messaging, and execution tracing across the system. It replaces unmanaged print() and direct logger calls with a structured, data-driven emission pipeline backed by a CSV string registry (utils/strings.csv).

| (main.py, nodes) |               |  Internal Registry |                         |

| Destination Router| <----------------------+                                    |

docs.title: Core Responsibilities
docs.text:
1. Structured Presentation: Decouples presentation logic from operational code by enforcing level-based ANSI color styling (PROGRESS, SUCCESS, WARNING, ERROR, INFO, DEBUG, FILE_WRITE, UI).
  2. Dual-Channel Dispatch: Directs output to standard output (STDOUT), disk-based log files (LOG), or both (BOTH), respecting severity mappings to Python's standard logging library.
  3. Internationalization & Localization (i18n): Translates user-facing messages and generated document titles dynamically using language-specific columns in utils/strings.csv.
  4. Autonomous Self-Healing Translations: Detects missing string translations at runtime, constructs translation prompts for target languages, invokes the LLM via call_llm.py, parses the structured JSON response, and persists translated strings back to strings.csv with UTF-8 BOM encoding.
  5. Per-Invocation File Logging: Configures dedicated timestamped log files in a configurable directory (logs/ by default) containing execution metadata and unstyled message streams.

docs.title: COLORS
docs.text:
COLORS = {
    "PROGRESS": "\033[96m",  # Cyan — LLM calls, active steps
    "SUCCESS": "\033[92m",  # Green — completions, cache hits
    "WARNING": "\033[93m",  # Yellow — warnings, capacity alerts
    "ERROR": "\033[91m",  # Red — errors, failures
    "INFO": "",  # Plain — config, counts, labels
    "DEBUG": "\033[90m",  # Gray — skipped files, debug
    "FILE_WRITE": "",  # Plain — "  - Wrote {path}" messages
    "UI": "",  # N/A — used in generated docs, never printed
}
Type: dict[str, str] Defines mapping from logical message levels to standard ANSI 8-bit escape sequences for terminal styling. Levels configured with empty strings ("") render without escape codes.

docs.title: RESET
docs.text:
RESET = "\033[0m"
Type: str The standard ANSI escape sequence used to reset terminal text attributes and colors back to default styling after emitting a colored message.

docs.title: LOG_LEVELS
docs.text:
LOG_LEVELS = {
    "PROGRESS": logging.INFO,
    "SUCCESS": logging.INFO,
    "WARNING": logging.WARNING,
    "ERROR": logging.ERROR,
    "INFO": logging.INFO,
    "DEBUG": logging.DEBUG,
    "FILE_WRITE": logging.DEBUG,
}
Type: dict[str, int] Maps user-facing logical emission levels to Python standard logging severity integer constants.

docs.title: Internal Module State Variables
docs.text:
• _strings: dict[str, dict[str, str]] — In-memory dictionary caching the parsed string registry. Keys are string identifiers (e.g., LLM_CALL_WRITE_CHAPTER), mapping to records containing {"text": str, "level": str, "dest": str}.
  • _language: str — Target display language capitalized for UI and logging outputs (e.g., "Vietnamese"). Defaults to "English".
  • _lang_col: str — Lowercase identifier matching CSV column header names (e.g., "vietnamese"). Defaults to "english".
  • _logger: logging.Logger — Named logger instance ("llm_logger") utilized across the application lifecycle.
  • _csv_path: str | None — Absolute filesystem path to utils/strings.csv. Initialized by init().
  • _use_cache: bool — Controls whether automated translation calls allow LLM prompt-response disk caching. Defaults to True.
  • _thinking_level: int | None — Configured LLM thinking or reasoning budget parameter forwarded to translation inference requests. Defaults to None.

docs.title: init()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def init(language: str = "english", use_cache: bool = True, thinking_level: int | None = None) -> None:

Description: Initializes the output subsystem. It resolves the absolute path to utils/strings.csv, sets module-level language preferences, populates the in-memory string lookup cache via _load_strings(), and triggers _auto_translate() to translate any missing localized strings via an LLM call before normal execution begins. Must be executed from the CLI entry point (main.py) after argument parsing but prior to any emit() calls.

Parameters: * language (str, optional): Target language for system messages and documentation generation. Defaults to "english". * use_cache (bool, optional): Flag indicating whether LLM calls for auto-translation should utilize the response cache. Defaults to True. * thinking_level (int | None, optional): Reasoning/thinking budget level forwarded to the LLM backend during translation. Defaults to None.

Returns: * None

Raises: * Does not raise exceptions directly; translation and file I/O exceptions during initialization are intercepted, logged as warnings, and fall back to English.

Implementation: 

def init(language="english", use_cache=True, thinking_level=None):
    global _language, _lang_col, _csv_path, _use_cache, _thinking_level
    _language = language.capitalize()
    _lang_col = language.lower()
    _csv_path = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)), "strings.csv")
    _use_cache = use_cache
    _thinking_level = thinking_level
    _load_strings()
    _auto_translate()

The function normalizes the input language parameter into capitalized form (_language) for human-readable logging and lowercase form (_lang_col) for column key lookups against strings.csv. It computes the absolute path to the CSV file relative to __file__, guaranteeing path consistency regardless of the current working directory. Once the internal globals are assigned, it executes a sequential load-and-translate sequence.

docs.title: emit()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def emit(key: str, suffix: str = "", **kwargs: Any) -> None:

Description: Emits a registered, localized message template to standard output, the log file, or both. The message is resolved from the internal string table by key, interpolated safely with provided keyword arguments (**kwargs), appended with an optional unformatted suffix, and decorated with ANSI terminal color codes corresponding to its declared severity level.

Parameters: * key (str): The unique string identifier defined in strings.csv (e.g., "LLM_CALL_WRITE_CHAPTER"). * suffix (str, optional): Additional text appended directly to the formatted message (e.g., token consumption statistics "(2,100 tokens)"). Defaults to "". * **kwargs (Any): Named replacement variables matching {placeholder} tokens in the template.

Returns: * None

Raises: * No exceptions raised. Unknown keys trigger an unstyled fallback warning directly to stdout ([UNKNOWN STRING: {key}]).

Implementation: 

def emit(key, suffix="", **kwargs):
    entry = _strings.get(key)
    if not entry:
        # Fallback for unknown keys — print raw so nothing is silently lost
        print(f"[UNKNOWN STRING: {key}]")
        return

    text = _format_safe(entry["text"], kwargs)
    if suffix:
        text = text + suffix

    level = entry["level"]
    dest = entry["dest"]
    color = COLORS.get(level, "")
    reset = RESET if color else ""

    if dest in ("BOTH", "STDOUT"):
        print(f"{color}{text}{reset}")
    if dest in ("BOTH", "LOG"):
        _logger.log(LOG_LEVELS.get(level, logging.INFO), text)

emit() performs a defensive dictionary lookup on _strings. If the requested key is not registered, it avoids raising KeyError or crashing the caller, opting to print [UNKNOWN STRING: <key>] to ensure the diagnostic failure is immediately visible. If the entry exists, it invokes _format_safe() to replace template placeholders, appends the raw suffix, maps the entry's destination attribute (dest) against allowed output targets (BOTH, STDOUT, LOG), and routes the unstyled text to _logger.log() while routing ANSI-wrapped text to print().

Example: 

# Real usage from source code docstring:
emit("LLM_CALL_WRITE_CHAPTER", chapter_num=1, name="flow")

docs.title: emit_raw()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def emit_raw(level: str, text: str, dest: str = "BOTH") -> None:

Description: Emits a pre-formatted, arbitrary string directly to the specified destination channel with ANSI level styling. This function bypasses strings.csv key lookups and is specifically designed for dynamic structural output such as tabular crawl statistics, raw error traces, progress counters, and dynamically formatted lists.

Parameters: * level (str): The severity level key (e.g., "PROGRESS", "SUCCESS", "WARNING", "ERROR", "DEBUG", "INFO"). * text (str): The pre-formatted text string to output. * dest (str, optional): Output destination routing. Allowed values are "BOTH", "STDOUT", or "LOG". Defaults to "BOTH".

Returns: * None

Raises: * No exceptions raised. Unmapped levels fall back to no ANSI color and standard logging.INFO.

Implementation: 

def emit_raw(level, text, dest="BOTH"):
    color = COLORS.get(level, "")
    reset = RESET if color else ""

    if dest in ("BOTH", "STDOUT"):
        print(f"{color}{text}{reset}")
    if dest in ("BOTH", "LOG"):
        _logger.log(LOG_LEVELS.get(level, logging.INFO), text)

emit_raw() enables arbitrary text emission while retaining visual consistency across the CLI. It queries COLORS and LOG_LEVELS directly using the provided level string. If dest includes stdout, it wraps text in ANSI color codes; if dest includes logging, it logs the plain uncolored text to ensure disk logs remain free of escape characters.

Example: 

# Real usage from source code docstring:
emit_raw("WARNING", "Custom message")

docs.title: get()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def get(key: str, **kwargs: Any) -> str:

Description: Retrieves a localized string template from the internal registry, applies variable formatting, and returns the raw string without emitting it to stdout or the log file. This function is primarily utilized by markdown-generating pipeline nodes (nodes.py) to fetch localized section headers, table titles, and UI text elements.

Parameters: * key (str): String key defined in strings.csv. * **kwargs (Any): Named parameters to interpolate into template placeholders.

Returns: * str: The translated, formatted string. If key is not found, the key itself is returned as a fallback.

Raises: * No exceptions raised.

Implementation: 

def get(key, **kwargs):
    entry = _strings.get(key)
    if not entry:
        return key  # Fallback: return the key itself
    return _format_safe(entry["text"], kwargs)

The get() function provides non-disruptive string resolution for document generation nodes. If the key exists in _strings, it delegates formatting to _format_safe(). If the key is missing, it defensively returns the raw key identifier string, ensuring downstream document assembly pipelines do not encounter NoneType errors or empty headings.

Example: 

# Real usage from source code docstring:
label = get("UI_TUTORIAL")

docs.title: configure_logging()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def configure_logging(project_name: str = "project", mode: str = "tutorial") -> str:

Description: Configures dedicated file-based logging for the active execution run. It resolves the target log directory (defaulting to the LOG_DIR environment variable or "logs"), sanitizes project and mode names for filesystem safety, creates a timestamped log file ({project}_{mode}_{YYYYMMDD_HHmmss}.log), clears existing handlers from _logger, attaches a formatted logging.FileHandler using UTF-8 encoding, and writes header metadata demarcating the start of the execution run.

Parameters: * project_name (str, optional): Name of the codebase project being processed. Non-alphanumeric characters (excluding -_..) are replaced with underscores. Defaults to "project". * mode (str, optional): Active pipeline operating mode (e.g., "tutorial", "deep-dive"). Hyphens are replaced with underscores. Defaults to "tutorial".

Returns: * str: The absolute or relative filesystem path to the newly created log file.

Raises: * OSError: If the target log directory cannot be created due to filesystem permissions.

Implementation: 

def configure_logging(project_name="project", mode="tutorial"):
    from datetime import datetime

    log_directory = os.getenv("LOG_DIR", "logs")
    os.makedirs(log_directory, exist_ok=True)

    safe_project = "".join(c if c.isalnum() or c in "-_." else "_" for c in project_name)
    safe_mode = mode.replace("-", "_")
    timestamp = datetime.now().strftime("%Y%m%d_%H%M%S")
    log_file = os.path.join(log_directory, f"{safe_project}_{safe_mode}_{timestamp}.log")

    # Remove any existing handlers (e.g., NullHandler) and add the file handler
    _logger.handlers.clear()
    file_handler = logging.FileHandler(log_file, encoding="utf-8")
    file_handler.setFormatter(logging.Formatter("%(asctime)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s"))
    _logger.addHandler(file_handler)

    # Log run metadata at the start of every log file
    _logger.info(f"{'=' * 80}")
    _logger.info(f"RUN STARTED | project={project_name} | mode={mode} | timestamp={timestamp}")
    _logger.info(f"Log file: {log_file}")
    _logger.info(f"{'=' * 80}")

    return log_file

configure_logging() isolates run logs into separate files, preventing log accumulation across multiple invocations. It replaces prior handlers on _logger (such as default stream handlers or NullHandler instances set during initial module import) with a single FileHandler configured for %(asctime)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s. It records initialization banners containing the un-sanitized project name, mode, and execution timestamp before returning the file path.

docs.title: _format_safe()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private Signature: def _format_safe(template: str, kwargs: dict[str, Any]) -> str:

Description: Safely applies Python string formatting (str.format(**kwargs)) against a template string. If the template contains unsupplied placeholders, malformed index markers, or invalid format specifiers, it intercepts KeyError, IndexError, and ValueError and returns the unmodified template.

Parameters: * template (str): Format string template potentially containing {key} placeholders. * kwargs (dict[str, Any]): Dictionary of substitution arguments.

Returns: * str: The successfully formatted string, or the raw template if interpolation raised an error.

Raises: * Intercepts all formatting exceptions (KeyError, IndexError, ValueError); never propagates errors.

Implementation: 

def _format_safe(template, kwargs):
    try:
        return template.format(**kwargs)
    except (KeyError, IndexError, ValueError):
        return template

This helper protects terminal rendering and document generation pipelines from formatting failures. In scenarios where a translated string modifies placeholder variable names or an API call omits an optional format argument, standard .format() would throw a fatal exception. _format_safe() guarantees graceful fallback by returning the raw string template.

docs.title: _load_strings()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private Signature: def _load_strings() -> None:

Description: Parses utils/strings.csv into the internal _strings dictionary cache. It ignores empty lines and comment rows (lines starting with #), reads metadata columns (LEVEL, DEST), extracts the target language translation matching _lang_col, and falls back to the "english" column if the target column is missing or empty. If all strings for a non-English language are successfully resolved, it emits a confirmation message.

Parameters: * None (operates on module-level globals _csv_path, _lang_col, _language, and _strings).

Returns: * None

Raises: * OSError: If the CSV file exists but cannot be read due to OS permission restrictions.

Implementation: 

def _load_strings():
    global _strings
    _strings = {}

    if not _csv_path or not os.path.exists(_csv_path):
        return

    translated_count = 0
    total_count = 0

    with open(_csv_path, encoding="utf-8-sig") as f:
        reader = csv.DictReader(f)
        for row in reader:
            key = row.get("STRING_KEY", "").strip()
            if not key or key.startswith("#"):
                continue

            level = row.get("LEVEL", "INFO").strip()
            dest = row.get("DEST", "BOTH").strip()

            # Priority: language column → English fallback
            text = row.get(_lang_col, "").strip()
            if text:
                translated_count += 1
            else:
                text = row.get("english", "").strip()

            total_count += 1
            _strings[key] = {"text": text, "level": level, "dest": dest}

    if _lang_col != "english" and translated_count == total_count:
        emit_raw("SUCCESS", f"[i18n] {_language} — loaded {translated_count} strings from CSV")

The function utilizes utf-8-sig encoding when reading strings.csv to strip Byte Order Marks (BOM) transparently. It tracks translated_count against total_count to determine whether all strings possess explicit translations for the requested language. If every key is translated and the selected language is not English, it emits a SUCCESS notification detailing the string count loaded.

docs.title: _auto_translate()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private Signature: def _auto_translate() -> None:

Description: Identifies untranslated strings in strings.csv for the active language, constructs an LLM prompt using prompts/common/translate_strings.md, calls call_llm() to obtain JSON-formatted translations, persists the new translations to disk via _write_translations_to_csv(), and triggers a cache reload via _load_strings().

Parameters: * None (uses module state _lang_col, _csv_path, _language, _use_cache, _thinking_level).

Returns: * None

Raises: * Catches all exceptions (Exception) during LLM invocation or JSON decoding, logs a warning message using emit_raw(), and falls back to English defaults.

Implementation: 

def _auto_translate():
    if _lang_col == "english":
        return

    if not _csv_path or not os.path.exists(_csv_path):
        return

    # Collect strings that have no translation in the target language column
    missing = {}
    is_new_column = False
    with open(_csv_path, encoding="utf-8-sig") as f:
        reader = csv.DictReader(f)
        fieldnames = list(reader.fieldnames)
        is_new_column = _lang_col not in fieldnames
        for row in reader:
            key = row.get("STRING_KEY", "").strip()
            if not key or key.startswith("#"):
                continue
            # Check if the language column exists and has a value
            lang_text = row.get(_lang_col, "").strip() if _lang_col in fieldnames else ""
            if lang_text:
                continue  # Already translated

            english_text = row.get("english", "").strip()
            if english_text:
                missing[key] = english_text

    if not missing:
        return

    # Report what we found
    if is_new_column:
        emit_raw("PROGRESS", f"[i18n] New language '{_language}' — adding column to strings.csv")
    emit_raw("PROGRESS", f"[i18n] {len(missing)} strings need translation to {_language}")

    # Batch translate via LLM
    try:
        from utils.call_llm import call_llm

        entries_json = json.dumps(missing, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2)

        # Load prompt template from prompts/common/translate_strings.md
        prompt_path = os.path.join(
            os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))),
            "prompts",
            "common",
            "translate_strings.md",
        )
        with open(prompt_path, encoding="utf-8") as pf:
            prompt_template = pf.read()
        prompt = prompt_template.format(language=_language, entries=entries_json)

        emit_raw("PROGRESS", f"[i18n] Calling LLM to translate {len(missing)} strings...")
        response = call_llm(prompt, use_cache=_use_cache, thinking_level=_thinking_level)

        # Extract JSON from response
        json_match = re.search(r"\{[^{}]*(?:\{[^{}]*\}[^{}]*)*\}", response, re.DOTALL)
        if json_match:
            translations = json.loads(json_match.group())
            translated_count = len(translations)

            # Write translations back into strings.csv
            _write_translations_to_csv(translations)
            emit_raw("SUCCESS", f"[i18n] Translated {translated_count}/{len(missing)} strings — saved to strings.csv")

            # Reload strings from the updated CSV so all translations are active
            _load_strings()
        else:
            emit_raw("WARNING", "[i18n] LLM response did not contain valid JSON — falling back to English")

    except Exception as e:
        emit_raw("WARNING", f"[i18n] Translation failed: {e} — falling back to English")

The function executes lazy translation initialization. It scans strings.csv to identify keys that lack values in the target column (_lang_col). If missing entries exist, it serializes them into a JSON payload and injects them into prompts/common/translate_strings.md. It executes an inference request through call_llm.py (call_llm()), extracts the JSON payload from the LLM response using regular expression matching (re.search(r"\{[^{}]*(?:\{[^{}]*\}[^{}]*)*\}", ...)), writes the translated records back to strings.csv, and triggers _load_strings() to activate the translations immediately.

docs.title: _write_translations_to_csv()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private Signature: def _write_translations_to_csv(translations: dict[str, str]) -> None:

Description: Updates utils/strings.csv on disk with newly generated translations. If the active language column does not exist in the CSV header, it is dynamically appended. The file is rewritten with utf-8-sig encoding (including a UTF-8 BOM) to ensure compatibility when opened directly in external spreadsheet applications like Microsoft Excel.

Parameters: * translations (dict[str, str]): Key-value dictionary where keys correspond to STRING_KEY identifiers and values contain translated strings.

Returns: * None

Raises: * OSError: If writing to _csv_path fails due to disk errors or file lock contentions.

Implementation: 

def _write_translations_to_csv(translations):
    rows = []
    fieldnames = None

    with open(_csv_path, encoding="utf-8-sig") as f:
        reader = csv.DictReader(f)
        fieldnames = list(reader.fieldnames)
        # Add language column if it doesn't exist
        if _lang_col not in fieldnames:
            fieldnames.append(_lang_col)
        for row in reader:
            key = row.get("STRING_KEY", "").strip()
            if key in translations:
                row[_lang_col] = translations[key]
            rows.append(row)

    # Write with BOM so Excel opens as UTF-8 without extra import steps
    with open(_csv_path, "w", encoding="utf-8-sig", newline="") as f:
        writer = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=fieldnames)
        writer.writeheader()
        writer.writerows(rows)

The function performs an in-place migration of strings.csv. It reads existing rows into memory, appends _lang_col to fieldnames if it is a newly introduced language, merges the incoming translations dictionary into matching row objects, and writes the entire dataset back out using csv.DictWriter. Setting encoding="utf-8-sig" ensures that multi-byte non-Latin characters (e.g., Vietnamese, Japanese, Chinese) render cleanly across all text editors and spreadsheet tools without encoding corruption.

docs.title: Data Schema: strings.csv
docs.text:
The strings.csv file defines the contract between string identifiers, emission levels, routing targets, and localized text.

Column Header Type Description STRING_KEY str Unique uppercase identifier (e.g., CRAWL_LOCAL_START, TOKEN_BUDGET_EXCEEDED). LEVEL str Message category matching COLORS and LOG_LEVELS (PROGRESS, SUCCESS, WARNING, ERROR, INFO, DEBUG, FILE_WRITE, UI). DEST str Target output sink (STDOUT, LOG, BOTH). english str Baseline English text containing {placeholder} variables. <language> str Dynamically appended columns for target languages (e.g., vietnamese, japanese, french).

docs.text:

  • crawl_local_files.py — Consumes emit() and emit_raw() to report filesystem traversal progress, skipped binary files, and crawl summaries.
  • crawl_github_files.py — Uses output.py to stream remote Git download statuses, API rate limit delays, and repository tree extraction metrics.
  • exclude_patterns.py — Baseline exclusion rules referenced by crawlers prior to emitting skip telemetry via output.py.
  • main.py — Initializes the output subsystem (init()) and configures file logging (configure_logging()) during CLI startup.
  • nodes.py — Utilizes get() to embed localized section headers into generated Markdown documentation files.

docs.title: utils.prompts
docs.text:
Source File Path: utils/prompts.py

The utils.prompts module contains reusable, programmatic prompt builders and documentation scaffolding utilities for internal system routines in Codebase-Knowledge-Builder. While mode-specific architectural prompts are loaded from structured external templates (prompts/{mode}/), utils.prompts manages programmatic prompt constructions for deterministic file filtering and cross-chapter contextual summarization, as well as configuration generators for local MkDocs exports (YAML config generation, Mermaid CSS overrides, and recursive navigation hierarchy construction).

docs.title: Architectural Role and Workflow
docs.text:
The functions in utils.prompts are utilized across distinct stages of the documentation pipeline:
